Historically, available data have been limited by their focus on general information, neglecting the specific needs of precise socioeconomic group assignments. In an effort to bridge this gap, we present a collection of large-scale digital records for the purpose of classifying individuals within precise socioeconomic categories. Comprising real-world transactions with detailed metric tracking, the dataset offers a unique view of consumers' purchasing behavior, allowing for the identification of targeted patterns that can aid in pinpointing exact socioeconomic standing. In addition, we present machine learning models that have been specifically designed to utilize only a limited set of socioeconomic-determining features, mimicking the purchasing habits of various socioeconomic groups. In this context, we term these features 'common' and 'distinctive,' with the former being commonly found across all socioeconomic groups and the latter being unique to each group. In an effort to train high-performing models without access to extensive training data that includes both sets of features, we present two novel unsupervised algorithms, the Clustering Purity Coder and the EM Classifier, that can classify socioeconomic groups with great precision. In a comprehensive digital record dataset, we demonstrate that by focusing on the unique features of each socioeconomic group, we can actually classify them with great precision, but run into difficulties when we also take into account the frequent occurrence of these same features across all socioeconomic groups. In an effort to train machine learning models that can utilize only the real-world transactions, we also present a solution that enables us to accurately classify individuals within precise socioeconomic groups. In this context, the Clustering Purity Coder produces a detailed mapping of the various socioeconomic groups and the real-world transactions that characterize each group. In an effort to train machine learning models that can classify individuals within socioeconomic groups, we also present a solution that enables us to accurately pinpoint the members of any given socioeconomic group simply by analyzing their real-world transactions. In this context, the EM Classifier achieves an impressive classification accuracy of 0.9406, thus demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed digital record and algorithmic framework in supporting the classification of individuals within precise socioeconomic groups. In an effort to further demonstrate the value of our proposed framework, we also present a large-scale digital record dataset that enables us to accurately classify individuals within 8 precise socioeconomic groups, with the aid of the Clustering Purity Coder and the EM Classifier. In this context, the digital record dataset and the proposed algorithms enable us to achieve an impressive classification accuracy of 0.9406.

However, as dataset volumes and complexities increase, the number of discovered patterns grows exponentially, overwhelming analysts with an extensive result space. Most existing algorithms and visualization methods fail to address this issue, making it challenging for users to effectively explore and understand the patterns in their data. To address this problem, we introduce a novel framework, called Hatcher, which is designed to efficiently and visually guide users through the pattern extraction process. By incorporating algorithms that utilize the structure of the data and efficient visualization, Hatcher provides a methodical approach to exploring the results, thus offering a significant improvement over existing solutions. Our approach is supported by a comprehensive study on the quality of Hatcher and a practical demonstration of its capabilities in the context of a real-world healthcare application. Furthermore, Hatcher is made available as an open-source tool, accessible via both command-line interface and interactive visualization, with the aim of promoting research in the area of algorithmic exploration and accountability. The source code for Hatcher can be found at https://github.com/milvio-hatcher/Hatcher, and we welcome contributions from the community. (Note: This work has been initially presented at PECOB 2020.) Nevertheless, its application to Torsion-based solids, also known as superconducting, topological crystal lattices, remains unclear. We resolve this ambiguity by demonstrating that the Torsion-based solids, featuring a lattice generated from two-dimensional lattice groups and integer scaling factors, adhere to Bloch's theorem. As a result, their electronic properties can be described using a lattice periodic, wave-vector-based (k-space-based) formulation. This conclusion is validated through direct confirmation of Bloch's theorem for all 40 Torsion-based single topological crystal lattices, including 12 single topological crystal lattices listed in the standard classification. Furthermore, our study showcases three Torsion-based compounds, showing that the electronic properties of these materials can be accurately represented using a lattice periodic, wave-vector-based (k-space-based) formulation. For example, in Torsion-based Cu$_3$PdN$_4$, a superconducting crystal lattice, the integer scaling factor corresponds to a new wave-vector $\mathbf{\tau}$. Interestingly, as a consequence of this wave-vector, the system's superconducting gap varies not only with the lattice potential, but also with this new wave-vector $\mathbf{\tau}$. Building on this evidence, a new wave-vector-based interaction Hamiltonian has been proposed within the framework of both perturbation theory and $G^0$ summation, both of which involve wave-vector $\mathbf{\tau}$. This provides a clear, integer scaling factor model for achieving novel properties and superconductivity through wave-vector $\mathbf{\tau}$ manipulation, suggesting the potential for $\mathbf{\tau}$ to be investigated as an additional control parameter in experiments. Overall, our findings rewrite the current understanding of Torsion-based solids and reveal the existence of an underlying, wave-vector-based (k-space-based) formulation that describes their electronic properties. This, in turn, offers new avenues in modulation techniques, allows comparison with other forms of 2D materials, and facilitates the use of wave-vector-based modulation in quantum experiments. Furthermore, our studies introduce the concept of employing wave-vector $\mathbf{\tau}$ as an new control parameter for exploring novel properties and superconductivity. We believe our research represents a major breakthrough in the field of Torsion-based solids, 2D materials, and quantum experiments. Researchers have been investigating constraint screening, a technique that can expedite the solution process for large-scale unit commitment problems by reducing the number of feasible solutions to consider. Current constraint screening methods rely on proprietary distribution networks and are adapted for optimal power distribution, not generation scheduling. This study demonstrates the applicability of constraint screening in generation scheduling by employing a machine learning model utilizing synthetic data and real-world generation network scenarios. Unlike previous approaches, our method focuses on the interactions between generators and considers the implications of constraints during the planning horizon, but also explores simplified representations for faster computation. A combination of three feature representations is tested, along with two machine learning models, and evaluated based on coverage and computational speed. Our findings, obtained from comprehensive simulations, confirm that our approach can effectively identify unviable solutions for unit commitment problems and substantially expedite the solution process, with potential accelerations of over two orders of magnitude in some cases. Importantly, we also establish that current distribution network constraint screening methods produce suboptimal results for generation scheduling and discuss the potential for future advancements. Additionally, this study highlights the importance of accounting for generator switches, thermal constraints, and other generator-specific features in constraint screening for unit commitment. As the electrical network continues to evolve toward direct integration of distributed generators, the proposed constraint screening method presents a valuable solution for transmission system operations, reducing the computational complexity of various generator scheduling problems. A corresponding source code is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/leandrocohen/css-uclargegen. This project also developed an open-access simulator in Pyomo, called SUIte, which facilitates the creation of unit commitment schedules with constraints based on generation network specifications. This simulator is available at the address https://pypi.org/project/suite/. Both the simulator and the constraint screening code are free to access, download, and utilize. A review of the existing constraint screening in power distribution networks can be found in the reference [1]. A study on the role of constraint screening in generation scheduling is presented in the reference [2]. A detailed analysis of the machine learning approach is reported in the reference [3]. A comparison of unit commitment solvers is reported in the reference [4]. A literature review on the application of machine learning in constraint screening for unit commitment is available in the reference [5]. To date, the constraint screening method has not been published in a journal. A corresponding study on direct constraint screening in generation scheduling was initially presented at the 2022 IEEE PowerEng Conference

The goal of synthetic control is to create a weighted average of units (supposedly similar to the treated entity) that, pre-intervention, mimic the treated entity's path. Initially used in trade disputes, this technique has also been applied in other fields such as medicine in treatment assessments and climate science in climate change analysis. Despite synthetic control's widespread use, concerns persist about its reliability. We suggest an alternative approach by formalizing the synthetic control method and treating it as an inverse problem to be addressed with Bayesian inference. By adopting a full Bayesian framework, users can quantify uncertainty in synthetic control estimates and assess the reliability of results. Our study provides a detailed explanation of the methodology and implements it in practical applications, which are accessible online. We also present two simulations and real-world examples to illustrate the added value of generating uncertainty distributions, such as confidence intervals, in particular scenarios. We draw a parallel to the uncertainty associated with carbon budget numbers regarding temperature and temperature increase. By adopting a 1.5 degrees Celsius temperature goal in line with the Paris Agreement, we can avoid irreversible damage from global warming and prevent massive loss of life, resources, and economic devastation. Carbon budget estimates represent a type of synthetic control where the "treated entity" is a global temperature, and the "inputs" are factors like fossil fuel use, deforestation, and land use changes. Furthermore, our approach can be utilized in any scenario where the intervention has a continuous effect. Building on the treated entity's historical data, we create a time-series forecast, generating a distribution of possible outcomes under different policies. Our model, a linear regression with industrial countries' historical data, is remarkably accurate in forecasting the treated entity's behavior. Our analysis of uncertainty distributions offers new insights in each application. By quantifying uncertainty in particular scenarios, we can refine the confidence level of results, identify scenarios with near-certainty, and recognize areas of significant uncertainty. In the context of the global warming treatment, our uncertainty distribution indicates a roughly 30% chance of avoiding irreversible damage from global warming if we stick to our current carbon emission trajectory. This outcome is based on the assumption that the treated entity is a global temperature, and the inputs are fossil fuel use, deforestation, and land use changes. In contrast, if we stick to a 1.5 degrees Celsius temperature goal in line with the Paris Agreement, we can avoid irreversible damage from global warming, as our model shows a distribution of possible outcomes under different policies

The smallest possible size of such a cover for ring $R$ is denoted as the covering number $\sigma(R)$,

For rings $R$ and $S$, when there is no inclusion relationship between them and their least cover sizes are both finite, this is known as a non-well-covered couple.

The authors of this study present various results regarding these concepts, achieving this by creating a new class of rings called $nAQ$.
From these results, it can be concluded that for rings $R$ with a covering number $\sigma(R)$ equal to a number greater than one, when $n_{AQ}(R)$ is sufficiently large, the least cover size of $R$ will be achieved by a cover of ring $R$.

In this paper, we establish that a particular architecture of neural networks, utilizing identity mappings, has a theoretical limit to contain errors stemming from malicious interference. However, in practical applications, these networks lose their capacity for constraint and consequently remain vulnerable to adversarial inputs. Similar reasoning can be applied to other deep neural networks featuring skip connections. Moreover, we show that a new class of deep neural networks, namely Neural ODEs, has a weaker constraint which prevents high-level interference but does not provide a clear boundary against adversarial inputs. Unlike standard deep neural networks, Neural ODEs appear more resistant to low-level attacks but experience comparable issues with high-level attacks. Existing defense methods have been found ineffective in preventing the emergence of new attacks, while neural networks with a weaker constraint such as Neural ODEs may provide a means for enhancing defense strategies without compromising accuracy. Historically, garbage collection has been used in functional languages, while imperative languages increasingly utilize type systems to safeguard memory usage. Our investigation applies existing methods for linear capabilities to ensure safe access to reference types that can be copied, with a particular emphasis on its novel extension to languages with tracing garbage collection, as well as data structures featuring explicit lifespan management. This work is related to hybrid programming that combines linear and non-linear capabilities, specifically in the context of the Rust language. Our study demonstrates that by utilising exclusive references with explicit borrowings, programming with capacity-constrained types can achieve memory safety even in the absence of a compiler-generated memory management framework, thereby enabling the automatic elimination of memory safety hazards. Moreover, we introduce a new programming pattern that assigns ownership of a data structure to the smallest possible pool of resources needed to prevent downcast hazards until more information becomes available. Consequently, with careful management of pointers and references, programming with capacity-constrained types can prevent downcast-related data corruption and crashes by ensuring that objects are not downgraded to a less-specific type. Our work is further substantiated by a state-of-the-art evaluation of existing imperative languages that ensure memory safety through type systems, specifically SML of Fine-grained Discrimination, Star, and RRB-style lists, as well as a novel extension to tracing garbage collection in Rust, namely Rust with RC groups. The evaluation shows that programming with capacity-constrained types can achieve significant safety improvements with minimal performance costs, making it a viable means of enforcing memory safety in a language without a compiler-generated memory management framework. The implementation details of our proposed technique are documented in an accompanying set of experimental software available at https://github.com/georgewhiting/gc-with-linear-capabilities, including the tooling used in our performance experiments at https://github.com/georgewhiting/early-RC-groups, as well as an initial prototype for translating Rust into a GC'd Rust with linear capabilities, based on a novel extension to Rust's RC groups, namely GC groups. The proposed model builds upon the Routh-Yawon-Zhilich (RYZ) model, which has demonstrated effectiveness in analyzing the dynamics of highly deformed and rapidly rotating nuclei. To generalize the RYZ model, we incorporate the Wigner-Eckart theorem, accounting for nuclear shape and angular momentum. The resulting expression for nuclear energy is expressed using the Zhitomirsky-Effeshev (ZE) method, which is equivalent to the Jost-Zimann (JZ) model. This examination highlighted the significance of coupling angles and magnetic masses in understanding these nuclei's characteristics. The theoretical framework has also enabled precise predictions regarding the behavior of energy thresholds, energy dips, and cruciform configurations observed in highly deformed and rapidly rotating nuclei. Additionally, we explored the relationship between magnetic masses and the deHaas-van Alphen effect in these nuclei, discovering that their magnetic oscillations conform to a standard generalized Sarma model. Notably, our theoretical framework also effectively explains the behavior of energy spectra in the exceptionally heavy rotating nucleus, $^{236}$U, which has been extensively studied experimentally. This research further solidifies our understanding of highly deformed and rapidly rotating nuclei and provides valuable insights for theoretical and experimental validation. Our focus in this paper lies on addressing a particular issue: providing access to referenced content such as citations, footnotes, images, tables, and mathematical equations. Unlike sighted individuals who can easily locate the referenced content, individuals who rely on linear audio narration find it extremely challenging. We suggest an approach based on visual detection to identify referenced content and gather necessary metadata that can be utilized in subsequent research to insert summaries into audio narratives. The technique we propose can effectively identify referenced content in scientific papers, mathematical theses, and educational handouts. It merely requires a single image per page without the need for page scraping. The technique has been autonomously applied to a 1.6 million document dataset without human intervention and has shown impressive results, achieving a 96.5% accuracy on a 2230-sample test set. The performance of the proposed approach is comparable to human experts who can identify referenced content with 95.8% accuracy. Furthermore, we have developed two algorithms that can autonomously insert summaries of referenced content. Results from a user study confirm that the quality of the summaries is satisfactory to the needs of print-disabled individuals. The proposed technique has immense potential for application across various fields such as science, engineering, and medicine. It has the added advantage of enabling research applications such as pinpointing locations of references on web pages and enabling search engines to index equations and diagrams like databases. Moreover, it can aid in protecting intellectual property by searching and locating sensitive content on web pages. Lastly, the proposed technique can aid in enabling artificial intelligence to comprehend the content of images, diagrams, and other visual content. The accompanying code is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository address: https://github.com/ashishjagani/Detection-of-Referenced-Content. A new pretraining approach, referred to as Mask-Aware BERT (MA-BERT), has been developed, which not only captures bidirectional contexts through masked token forecasting but also leverages the privileged knowledge of unmasked tokens. Furthermore, MA-BERT proposes a novel objective, masked-grouping, which takes into account the grouping effect in masked tokens under bidirectional attention guidance, thereby generating a comprehensive representation. Upon pretraining with the proposed strategy, MA-BERT demonstrates superior performance on various tasks and datasets compared to or without group-aware objectives. Moreover, incorporating MA-BERT into the fine-tuning stage yields state-of-the-art results on six datasets, highlighting its effectiveness. By further examining MA-BERT's behavior, it becomes evident that suppressing unprivileged context information enhances the model's ability to learn a task-specific representation, thus leading to better performance in fine-tuning. In light of these findings, we recommend using MA-BERT as a replacement for traditional BERT in both pretraining and fine-tuning operations. Our code is available at https://github.com/yangwei1211/MABERT. We also introduce six general unsupervised language models, which utilize unique tasks including word ordering, word reversal, word size-based grouping, syntactic grouping, sentence grouping, and paraphrasing. Our experiments show that MA-BERT-SYN and MA-BERT achieve comparable performance. However, MA-BERT-SYN offers the advantage of processing sequences more quickly than MA-BERT. Our analysis confirms that modeling bidirectional attention is crucial for pretraining, and the group-based objectives play a key role in bidirectional attention pretraining. We also found that pretraining with both masking and grouping objectives of BERT significantly improves the model's ability to capture the grouping effect in masked tokens, even when the group size approaches the number of masked tokens. We've analyzed models representing three archetypal planetary systems, including a Jupiter-like world, a Neptune-like one, and a terrestrial exoplanim, using simulated stellar spectra, both with and without realistic impairments, and with and without the presence of a planet. We introduce a novel framework for evaluating system resiliency based on a specific logical structure called a Resiliency Specification, which is comprised of STL formulas. By integrating time bounds and combining individual components, this framework provides an in-depth analysis of a system's ability to rapidly recover and maintain stability. We provide a measurable Resilience Satisfaction Value, which evaluates resiliency on a scale, considering two key factors: swift recovery from disturbances and sustained stability. The practicality of our approach is demonstrated by the development of scalable computation methods for the RSValue of a system's local fragment. This marks a significant advancement in the field of formal resiliency analysis, as none of the existing methods consider the recovery aspect of resiliency. We test our framework using case studies, such as a control algorithm for a cylinder and a heating, ventilation, and cooling system, to illustrate the accuracy and efficiency of computation. Furthermore, our framework allows for the computation of an approximation value in a reasonable amount of time, supported by our results from the case studies. Building upon existing work in runtime monitoring, we introduce resiliency-aware monitoring, which can be used to tackle real-time resiliency assessment, provided that the time bounds are adjusted. However, if the system's response time is insufficient to fulfill the required resiliency level, our method allows for an online adjustment of the time bounds, which in turn affects the requirement for resiliency. We demonstrate the process using the cylinder system example, which showcases the adaptability of our framework. The code used in this research is publicly available on GitHub. Based on our findings, we strongly believe that our framework can successfully analyze and assess the resiliency of Cyber-Physical Systems and inform software developers in real-time, contributing valuable knowledge to the field of resiliency software development. The uniqueness of our framework lies in its ability to simultaneously evaluate a system's rapid recovery and sustained stability. Moreover, our framework features scalable computation methods, supported by our results from the case studies, which show the feasibility of resiliency analysis. The emergence of our framework marks a significant milestone, offering for the first time a practical approach to formally assess the resiliency of Cyber-Physical Systems, specifically targeting those with nonlinear behavior and with the ability to be monitored in real-time. The resilience analysis algorithm can also be applied to non-real-time systems in the field of transportation, such as traffic light systems, with the added benefit of our software being publicly available on GitHub.

It finds a strong correlation between polarization and source size below ~5", with a weaker correlation above ~8". The results indicate depolarization due to the host galaxy and surrounding environment. Additionally, the curvature of low-frequency radio spectra shows an inverse correlation with polarization. Most sources experience significant source-size-dependent depolarization, along with less pronounced scale-dependent polarization, suggesting that these effects are intertwined with source evolution. Existing models based on source size need revision to account for the complex processes at play. The analysis also confirms past results that indicate a strong correlation between polarization and curvature, with a need to consider instrumental effects in order to make accurate measurements. This specification is rendered possible through the decomposition of the conditioning distribution into its stationary and non-stationary components, representing the typical and atypical characteristics, respectively. We illustrate the effectiveness of this method using a simulated scenario modeling the behavior of a population of agents responding to diverse stimuli. Lastly, we apply the developed approach to a real-world case study involving the analysis of price response in electricity markets. This was accomplished by incorporating the established method for hand-specifying the conditioning distribution into a extended Variational Inference algorithm originally designed for the analysis of time-series data conditioned on past observations. The results from both the simulated and real-world datasets indicate that incorporating the hand-specified conditioning distribution can substantially boost the reconstructed trajectory's accuracy, particularly its quasi-stationary equilibrium, as validated through comparisons with models utilizing solely the hand-specified conditioning distribution and those that do not account for conditioning variability. In conclusion, the discussion highlights potential avenues for expanding the existing methodology in both theory and practice. Initially, this involves exploring the use of deep neural networks to dynamically hand-specify the conditioning distribution in response to time-varying stimuli. Secondly, the study of quasi-stationary dynamics provides a novel framework for modeling and describing the behavior of complex systems subject to external influences. Numerous examples demonstrate the vast applicability of the developed theory, spanning from modeling the behavior of populations and networks to understanding molecular dynamics and the behavior of macromolecules. Lastly, the investigation of conditioning distributions offers a fresh and innovative approach for interpreting the results of existing simulation studies in the fields of economics, biology, chemistry, and physics. Nonetheless, a major constraint of the established theory is its requirement that the system must be able to transition between its typical states. We have proposed an extension of the theory that does not impose this requirement, and the accompanying text provides a concrete example of this relaxation by conditioning the dynamics of a single molecule on its initial state. The developed approach is further supported by numerical simulations, and the inherent parameters of the system can be deduced through the analysis of the reconstructed distribution, ensuring that the quasi-stationary assumption does not compromise the accuracy of the reconstruction. We propose a novel variant of federated learning known as sorted federated learning that leverages non-parametric density estimation and kernel methods to safeguard individual data points. Unlike existing sorts that depend on the data distribution, our algorithm can perform sorting on randomly collected data, thereby reducing communication and enhancing privacy. We rigorously analyze the theoretical properties of this innovation and confirm its effectiveness through comprehensive numerical simulations on both artificial and real-world datasets. Furthermore, our research reveals that sorted federated learning achieves better classification performance on a range of test datasets with substantially reduced communication efforts compared to its traditional counterpart. Moreover, our algorithm satisfies local differential privacy at zero cost while maintaining comparable classification precision on several test datasets. Finally, our numerical observations demonstrate the considerable potential of sorted federated learning for enhancing both privacy and inference accuracy. 
This research can be further enhanced by applying sorted federated learning to unlabelled data and exploring more sophisticated data representation methods such as graph-based kernels in the future. 
The related code can be found at this repository address: https://github.com/mil-ai/Sort-Fed-Learn. 
The presented work has significant practical value primarily because it tackles a crucial challenge in the field of machine learning: the labeled data problem. To address this, we conducted experiments on adding noise to the labels and demonstrated that sorted federated learning can successfully recover the ground truth labelling with minimal communication. This application has real-world implications as the labelling process itself poses a significant privacy risk. We have already started exploring ways to apply sorted federated learning to tackle labelling issues in a privacy-preserving manner.

This research proposes a novel two-stage approach using a genetic algorithm (GA) to generate user-specific sequences for grant-free uplink access. In the first stage, the initial GA finds a population of ideal sequence densities that balance both randomizing and concentrating phases. Then, in the second stage, a joint genetic-hill-climbing algorithm fine-tunes the distribution to minimize interference from others in each time slot, and from the channel, to maximize the average transmission rate. Results show that the proposed method outperforms the standard genetic algorithm, especially when many users contend for the channel. Additionally, the hill-climbing algorithm surpasses the initial GA in each stage. Our technique outperforms the benchmark as well as other known methods, including the weighted minimum entropy of power spectrum and the genetic algorithm used for sequence optimization, and a method using joint genetic-algorithms for both power spectrum and phase coding. Moreover, the paper opens the door to utilizing indirect learning to enhance the performance of mMTC grant-free uplink access. This includes combining the learned power spectrum with the genetic-algorithm-based sequence design to improve the mean achievable sum rate, even when the available average SNR is low. This is verified through simulated results showing a performance gain when using the learned power spectrum in mMTC. This research has successfully applied the hill-climbing algorithm in the context of genetic algorithm for sequence design to tackle both high and low SNR scenarios. This is the first time such an application has been utilized as a baseline in this context. As such, the proposed two-stage hill-climbing algorithm can be a more effective genetic algorithm for sequence design to be used as a baseline in this setting. This research has the potential to enhance the performance of genetic algorithms for sequence design in various applications, as well as being more suitable for wireless communications, where learning can occur. This is because the learned results from one situation can be applied in another to improve performance. Such cross-learning applications include both short-term and long-term learning, where the genetic-algorithm-based sequence design results from such can be utilized for optimizing mMTC grant-free uplink access. This is because there is currently a lack of knowledge in this area and the learned results can be from one scenario and applied in another to improve performance. Results show that the proposed two-stage hill-climbing algorithm can enhance the understanding of genetic algorithms for sequence design and support the development of learning-based communication technologies

Nevertheless, confusion networks (a more complex set of possible outcomes than a shortlist) can be a compact representation of the potential outcomes of the system.  We investigate in this study the advantages of using confusion networks with the aid of the most up-to-date neural system designed to follow dialogue (a dialogue state tracker) - specifically one model known as the GLAD model.  We have developed an approach that translates two-dimensional confusion networks into one-dimensional sequences of vectors (embeddings) through the application of a type of neural network known as an attentional confusion network encoder - a type of neural network that can be integrated with virtually any existing dialogue state tracking model.  We discovered substantial gains in performance when this new method is used instead of the typical ASR hypotheses list, including better precision and a reduction in computation time, when combined with the GLAD model for the task of following dialogue flow.  We also found that this new method is benefits from being integrated early in the system, when the possible outcomes are simpler, resulting in better dialogue flow prediction.  We have also developed an approach that translates confusion networks into a list of the top outcomes, allowing for a more accurate prediction of the top dialogue flow when the system is confused, resulting in better precision and a reduction in computation time for the prediction of dialogue flow, with the highest gains in the more complex dialogue scenarios.  We have thoroughly tested our method by applying it to real-world data and a particular type of conversation about appointments, and have visualized the results of the method by translating the possible outcomes into a list of the top outcomes for a type of dialogue about appointments in order to make the results clearer and more understandable. Specifically, this structure contains participants in all feasible Boolean combinations of the minimal qualified subsets, yielding the maximum complexity given the number of subsets. Every access structure can be considered a subset of this universal structure when having the same number of minimal qualified subsets, thereby the universal access structure possesses the highest complexity given the subset count. representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. These techniques primarily address the issue of feature shift, which arises when the distribution of data evolves over time. However, the challenge of class shift, which occurs when new classes are added and old ones reassigned, is underexplored. In this paper, we present a novel approach called Class-aware Re Representation (CARR) to deal with the problem of class shift in continual learning. CARR aims to mitigate the effect of shifts in class distributions by modifying the embedding of the final fully connected layer of a pre-trained model. We initially identify the class bias by comparing the average representations of each class's samples, then adjust the representations by subtracting the class bias on the oldest class. We evaluate CARR on benchmark datasets and our results show that CARR achieves superior performance compared to the existing state-of-the-art approaches. The source code of CARR is available on GitHub.

researchers have focused on tackling the pervasive issue of hate speech online. This pernicious problem gives rise to real-world consequences, such as heightened social divisions and violent crimes. Previous studies have employed automated hate speech detection methods, but they often fall short by overlooking broader social and contextual nuances. Furthermore, few attempts have been made to embed hate speech understanding within large language models, thereby limiting their practical application in multi-language, multi-category, and multi-cultural contexts. Our research endeavors address these shortcomings by proposing a context-aware and deeply learned hate speech classification model, known as Gauging Contextual Similarity (GeCS), which accurately identifies hate speech in multiple languages and recognizes subtle social signs. Unlike traditional neural network models, GNN can operate in a decentralized manner, facilitating communication among neighboring nodes and potentially leading to more efficient control mechanisms in wireless communication systems. However, wireless channel disruptions significantly reduce the robustness of GNN predictions. To overcome this limitation, we propose learning a robust GNN that incorporates the characteristics of wireless communication channels. By equipping the GNN with wireless communication channel information, we use the Least Squares Temporal Delayed Identification (LSTDI) method to finetune the GNN's parameters, thus increasing its robustness and effectiveness. We validate our approach by creating a large-scale dataset based on a real-world power grid, demonstrating that the robust GNN can maintain its accuracy in the presence of communication disruptions, whereas conventional GNN experiences a substantial decline in performance. Simulation results show that our method performs better than existing methods and achieves a notable improvement in robustness and accuracy. Notably, we provide a closed-form expression for the theoretical upper bound of the robustness of our method. Furthermore, we establish a performance verification metric that assesses the effectiveness of our approach and verify through experiments that the obtained robust GNN can operate under decentralized conditions with reduced communication disruptions. As the research domain of wireless communication and machine learning is rapidly growing, our technique has potential to be translated into other research studies involving GNN-based wireless communication systems. Detailed information about our experiment is made accessible through a publicly available dataset on datasets.hop.io. Research has shown that these patterns, specifically in shrublands, offer protection from erosion by slowing wind down, which can lead to the growth of new plants in previously barren areas. This text outlines a simplified game-theoretic approach using the two-player game known as the "battle of the sexes," modified to assess how developers and users of non-quantum "quantum-like" communication technologies interact. This modified game involves nodes connected by a simulated, delayed quantum channel. Since actual quantum channels are not yet available, such simulations are a practical means of testing the potential of innovative technologies. They help address a key challenge: whether to invest substantial resources in new technologies or take advantage of early access to functional prototypes. This decision is crucial both for companies that develop the technology and for companies that might benefit from it. By employing the theory of Nash games, we examine strategies for different game players that do not require prior knowledge of the other players' behavior. A numerical simulation illustrates the application of this approach to two-player games. Given that true quantum games are not yet feasible, this project also considers how to use existing non-quantum resources to create simulated quantum games. A proposed design involves the "quantum-like" use of coherent states from two independent lasers to transfer data through a simulated light path. This would allow users to test the strategies and decisions resulting from interactions involving "quantum-like" states, without the actual need for a quantum computer. Building on the principles of optical communication, where signals are typically short and transient, we use the concept of the joint amplitude probability distribution to assess the potential of different game strategies. However, due to the inherent imperfections of real-world systems, any experimental attempt to replicate the desired quantum-like behavior would likely fail. Instead, we argue that the principal goal should be to create truly random entangled states, rather than attempting to preserve individual coherent states for extended periods. To achieve this, we propose a scheme that leverages fundamental quantum noise to produce entangled states. Importantly, our proposed approach focuses on the distribution of entangled states, rather than attempting to control the individual components, thereby facilitating the development of innovative technologies that minimize investment in time and resources. While true quantum games remain a distant prospect, our proposed approaches - the game-theoretic analysis of quasi-quantum communication and the design of random entangled state generators - represent meaningful milestones towards the creation of the first practical quantum communication networks. The aim is to develop robust auction designs that don't rely on the buyer-demand distribution and work well across diverse contract scenarios between intermediaries and buyers.

Initially, we focus on the case of $k$ identical items where buyers draw private valuations independently from a specified distribution, known as a $\lambda$-regular distribution. By designing a straightforward posted-price mechanism that determines per-item prices based on $k$ and the total number of buyers, we create a mechanism that can achieve nearly optimal revenue regardless of the buyer-demand distribution and certain contract requirements. 

We then extend our work to the case of distinct items. By employing the assumption of separable item valuations and using a menu of posted prices, we design a mechanism that can attain at least a fraction of the optimal welfare, independent of the buyer-demand distribution, though our solution makes a stronger assumption about the distribution. Our results yield new insights and a tight bound on the impact of uncertain buyer-demand on posted-price mechanisms. Additionally, our work highlights a posted-price mechanism that can near-optimally maximise welfare in the scenario of distinct items with separable valuations, assuming all possible buyer scenarios.

Specifically, it is demonstrated that the estimate's distribution converges asymptotically to a Gaussian distribution with mean zero, with a standard deviation calculated as the square root of the sum of squares of individual component variances. Euler characteristic is a fundamental, widely recognized topological invariant with numerous past uses, especially in studies involving random fields. Our primary objective is to illustrate its application in high-dimensional spaces. While employing more powerful invariants like homology remains an active area of research, the theoretical and computational feasibility of the Euler characteristic make it an attractive intermediate step for multi-variable topological analysis. We demonstrate its practicality by using artificial datasets and a real-world example involving diabetic retinopathy detection from retinal images. The supporting code for this research has been made available on the Git repository: https://github.com/dgandallo/ETDA. It includes code written in Python 3 for data generation, computation, and visualization, utilizing packages like scikit-learn, SciPy, and Plotly. The repository also contains a document outlining the methods and a supplementary document containing additional figures and tables to enhance understanding. A Docker image has been created to facilitate easy reproduction of the results. The project's main components are hosted on GitHub. As a secondary outcome, this study shows that using the Euler characteristic for TDA on challenging synthetic datasets can be effective, but confirm that the method has limitations on a specific real-world medical task and therefore should not be used in that particular application. The findings highlight the importance of choosing the appropriate topological measure for a particular analysis. We suggest employing the Euler characteristic as an efficient and straightforward preliminary step to establish a baseline for more sophisticated models. Our code also shows that noise reduction is a key factor for successful ETDA. We propose using the Euler characteristic for preliminary processing, then reformatting the data into an efficient form for analysis. The study shows that ETDA has the potential for strong classification while using the original data format, but using the Euler characteristic as an internal tool significantly improves understanding of the power of TDA in its simplest form. The project's main value lies in its educational significance: the study shows that the Euler characteristic has notable analytical power, but it is limited compared to more advanced computational approaches. We suggest ETDA as an efficient way to establish a baseline for more sophisticated computational topological analysis, and hope this study brings more awareness to the use of Euler characteristic as a preliminary step in TDA. As for the direct application, we found that the studied medical condition, diabetic retinopathy, is not well-identified using the ETDA approach, and a more sophisticated method, such as deep learning, is preferred for higher accuracy. 2017-BLG-1434 involved a cold super-Earth planet located among Galactic bulge stars, where the anomaly was eliminated after taking into account the effects of a companion of comparable mass.  A parametric analysis using the Galaxyscope software further confirmed the existence of this secondary object.  With a mass equivalent to approximately 0.00003 solar masses, this cause for the anomaly is among the lightest micro-lens companions yet detected.  With the aid of the Galaxyscope software, a system configuration was identified, where the primary object has a mass around 0.23 times that of Earth and resides 3.27 mas from the observer's view.  The relative positions of the two objects are nearly aligned in the direction of the observer's view.  Light coming from the observer's view is blocked entirely by the secondary object's gravitational field.  What remains unexplained in the data could not be accounted for by the studied system's effects alone; rather, it may be the result of additional, unaccounted micro-lens objects, possibly at significantly different positions within the observer's view's field.  An additional possibility exists that a small binary system, possibly containing a tilted binary, lies at a significant distance from the observer's view.  Further research, such as radial velocity analysis, is needed to confirm the existence of the secondary object and uncover the remaining truth about OGLE-2017-BLG-1434.

A sequence of strategic clicks leads to winning, which means turning off all lights in a predetermined number of clicks. Inspired by the original Lights Out game from Tiger Electronics, we're investigating an extension known as the Most Clicks Problem, which involves identifying the most clicks required to solve any given configuration of lights in a grid-based graph. Given our analysis, we've developed a polynomial-time algorithm to compute an optimal solution, which involves flipping three lights in a single step, and our results demonstrate that this method is also efficient for solving original Lights Out puzzles. Moreover, we've developed a constant-factor approximation algorithm for solving puzzles that require four clicks, and our experiments show that we can reliably and efficiently compute a close solution via local search. Interestingly, we've found a counterintuitive property: the most clicks required to solve a puzzle doesn't necessarily increase as you move away from it in the Levenshtein distance, which measures the least cost of edits needed to transform one string into another. as data mining and machine learning relies heavily on distance-based methods due to their adaptability in generic metric spaces. Large-scale data processing in these fields requires more efficient algorithms to handle high-dimensional datasets effectively. A fundamental distance measure, Mahalanobis distance, is a linear combination of traditional distance metrics and has been proven to be outperforming conventional methods like $k$-means or $k$-medoids for specific settings. This study presents a new algorithm for detecting outliers based on modified Mahalanobis distance, which also serves as a feasible approximation for the conventional distance metric. The proposed algorithm incorporates a selective sampling strategy, enables outlier detection without requiring a predefined number of outliers, and achieves this process efficiently by pruning unnecessary clusters. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves superior accuracy and time complexity compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we provide theoretical proof that our algorithm's expected time complexity is optimal. The proposed method has been successfully tested on various real-world datasets and is currently integrated into a scalable system for large-scale outlier detection. This system includes practical utility functions for data sampling, scoring, and batch processing. As an alternative algorithm, we present a simple yet efficient method for detecting outliers using mutual nearest neighbors, which involves simply removing the majority vote winner from each cluster's core. Experimental results show that this basic algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods like DBSCAN and FastABC. The core concept of sampling has been utilized here to provide a clean and robust algorithm for outlier detection. This new approach has been validated across various datasets and provides a simple alternative to current methods. The implementation of this algorithm is available online at https://github.com/acowgill/OptMahalanobis for public use. Similarly, the system containing the utility functions for data sampling, scoring, and batch processing is available at https://github.com/acowgill/SimpleOutlierDetection. particularly for tasks defined by interactive information, the framework of episodic reinforcement learning is often used to train agents and maintain diversity of experiences between episodes.  However, existing methods still struggle with ensuring sufficient representative data within local memory pools, given the absence of a universal measure to gauge this data's usefulness.  As a result, the representation distribution of this memory varies greatly between agents, leading to less optimal data sharing among neighbors in a network and a lack of representation uniformity within each agent's local pool.  To address this, the current work introduces a novel data representation approach, which utilizes the mutual information between adjacent agents to standardize their shared experience and promote representation diversity within individual memory pools.  We test the efficacy of this method, dubbed MR2, across multiple neural-lifetime learning scenarios and find that it effectively facilitates representation sharing among agents and uniformity within individual pools. Upon increasing this cost, the Toric code progresses from a fully charged to a code-degenerate state, exhibiting a phase shift characterized by shrinking codes over time. This shift can be seen in the increasing importance of existing knowledge graphs, which can be utilized to bridge the gap between language capabilities and world knowledge. Nevertheless, most existing models struggle to capture diverse and complex world knowledge, primarily due to their reliance on static knowledge graphs, which can't effectively address knowledge gaps encountered during training and inference. However, the standard approach to FNE incurs significant repetition and redundancy in labeling, as it relies on categorizing each entity first into a broader group and then into sub-categories, resulting in a doubling of label counts. To circumvent this issue, the current challenge focuses on using plain NER labels, reducing the label space and consequently the number of parameters, and in turn, enhancing the challenge's overall accuracy. Building on this concept, our proposed method employs two separate model components, a shared encoder and two decoders, to distinguish between coarse and fine labels, and assign specific labels to entities, thus leveraging information from multiple perspectives. The strategy not only decreases repetition in labeling but also enables the models to learn from the unique relationships between the two label sets. Experimental findings on multiple datasets show that our proposed method outperforms the existing state-of-the-art approach. Compared to traditional autoencoders, VAEs exhibit enhanced reconstructive capabilities, making more accurate approximations possible even in the presence of noise, as opposed to Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. By utilizing a hierarchical series of probabilistic layers, VAEs formulate a generative process that involves ancestral sampling, thus serving as directed graphical models. Each VAE component can be interpreted as a probabilistic neural network, with its parameters optimized through the application of stochastic gradient descent to produce a more accurate distributional representation. Although VAE learning is facilitated by the presence of a key regularization term, the reward signal it provides is weak and limited in scope. Consequently, when the underlying distribution exhibits significant shifts or has uncertain or undefined probability densities, the learning process is hindered or made impossible with standard off-the-shelf VAEs. VAEs show remarkable promise in numerous domains, yet their practical application in a wide range of real-world scenarios is hindered by their dependence on optimal component learning. As an innovative solution to this challenge, we introduce the Adaptive Variational Network (AdVaN), an advanced real-time adaptive framework capable of learning corresponding probability distributions over continuous rewards and action spaces. Using the generative capabilities of VAEs, we achieve crucial aspects of our framework: undetermined density estimation and adaptive learning, thus producing accurate distributional representations. Through Monte Carlo sampling, we provide explicit reward quantification, along with a generative flow for downstream applications in fields such as quality control, forecasting, and decision-making. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the capability of the AdVaN reward estimator to adapt to different and unknown density distributions on both synthetic and real-world data. It outperforms competing methods in reward extraction, significantly exceeding expectations in complex scenarios where the distribution is both shifting and unknown. It was discovered that average L-values of QAM symbols consistently adhere to an ordered relationship, which facilitated the design of a deep autoencoder. This autoencoder simultaneously compresses and separately reconstructs L-values using a weighted loss function prioritizing successful reconstruction of the top percentile of L-values, which correspond to most commonly occurring states. Simulation results indicate that the proposed method rivals the performance of arithmetic coding while requiring fewer bits. Specifically, at a 0.999 success rate, the proposed method achieves a 0.4 dB gain over arithmetic coding, with a reduction of 0.16 bits per symbol. This achievement is without reliance on specific channel knowledge, making it suitable for scenarios where channel information is limited or dynamic. The associated L-values are suitable for use in channels with rapidly changing, unknown, or limited knowledge availability. The proposed method has been awarded the 2021 best paper award at the IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory. The proposed method has been pre-qualified for cases where the base QAM signal has known, Gaussian channel conditions. Nonetheless, the deep autoencoder used is independent of the specific channel conditions, allowing it to be adapted for other scenarios where the L-values may deviate from those produced under Gaussian assumptions. This is corroborated by simulation results showing the proposed method's resilience in L-values produced by a Rayleigh block-fading environment following an outage event over a 4-QAM, 16-QAM, and 64-QAM base signal. The proposed method's performance is also evaluated in hybrid wireless channels with simultaneous use of a wireless channel and a dispersive optical channel, with the optical channel having a bandwidth much larger than the wireless channel. By formulating interconversion conditions for these resources, we have developed a generalisation of the first law of thermodynamics. Our research demonstrates that, despite the added complexity, the first law of thermodynamics for multiple resources remains straightforward to derive. In the quantum regime, the conserved quantity is explicitly expressed in terms of the physical system's state and its corresponding quantum states called 'purifiers.' We have further found that the first law remains accessible even in more advanced scenarios, including when the purifiers depend on the system and its surroundings, and when the system's quantum state is described imprecisely. Our research has theoretical implications for understanding the management of quantum information and thermodynamic properties, and may yield practical applications in the accurate measurement of conserved quantities, such as electric charge. The approach presented here sets the stage for future investigations into more intricate scenarios. As an example of this, we also examined a case where the first law of thermodynamics is disrupted due to the system's quantum state being described imprecisely, known as'missing information.' Our research found that, in this scenario, the physical system's quantum state can be restored by refining its description using an entangled state. This process relies on the system's quantum entanglement with a larger system, known as 'thermodynamic entropy,' which makes it more difficult to acquire the information associated with this entropy. As a result, our research proposes a broader understanding of thermodynamic entropy that encompasses not only the imprecision in one's description of the system but also any imprecision held by a suitable entangled state. Furthermore, our research sets the stage for future investigations into scenarios with multiple, interconnected information resources that remain a topic of study in active research. In particular, our research proposes the discovery of new, previously unrecognized forms of information that may emerge due to the interaction of distinct information resources. A key aspect of this structure lies in the utilization of constant-size random codes mapping $m$-bit vectors to $\Delta m$-bit vectors. We explore two specific scenarios: one focusing on the relationship between bulk and corner states, and the other examining edge and corner correlations. We establish the existence of mobility gaps for bulk-corner correspondence and clarify the topological properties defining these gaps. Interestingly, our study reveals that while bulk-corner correspondence is insensitive to disorder; corner states are highly dependent on it. We also find that, in a 3D topological insulator of order three, disorder has no impact on the coupling between edge and corner states. Notably, our investigation supports the view that corner states in these topological insulators can be considered as'mobile' corners. Lastly, our research provides a foundation for future studies on the behavior of corner states under both disorder and electric fields within the bulk. Specifically, we propose a new phase of 'frozen' corners, and the possibility of modulating corner states via external influences is also explored. This work was inspired and concluded as part of a doctoral thesis. As such, it draws upon existing research but also presents new findings that extend our understanding of the subject. We delve into the specifics of a specific system, in which a 2D topological insulator of order three is connected to a 1D wire on both 3D and 2D systems. A notable discovery is that while bulk-corner correspondence in 2D systems remains unaffected by disorder, corner states become effectively'mobile'. We refer to these as quasi-states. Furthermore, our research reveals that these quasi-states can transition into full corner states through the application of a local electric field, or return to the quasi-state as the field is removed. We propose the use of scanning tunneling microscopy to directly observe the impact of disorder on the bulk-corner correspondence, and the potential of applying a local electric field to modulate the behavior of corner states. This work also extends our understanding of the mobility of corner states, and the possibility of achieving a new phase of the material in which electric field application leads to the localized confinement of a second set of corner states. We refer to this as the 'Frozen Corner' phase, and the characteristic features defining this phase, along with the conditions required to achieve it, are outlined within this research. An investigation into a specific system is presented, and the results show that the 'Frozen Corner' phase can be successfully realized. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks. Notably, our findings show that using an unbalanced mixture of states does not hinder class separation on the quantum plane, allowing for effective classification. We also observe that, despite some similarities, K-means and quantum support vector machine exhibit different behavior. Moreover, our classification outcomes are resistant to specific types of quantum noise, differing from quantum support vector machine behavior under identical noise conditions. We propose a future research plan to compare the efficiency of these algorithms, potentially leveraging near-term quantum hardware. This work highlights the potential for existing machine learning methods to be translated on near-term quantum hardware, potentially leveraging their inherent properties and allowing for direct mapping to quantum circuits. Future studies could explore applying these algorithms to various quantum systems or using them as building blocks for more complex quantum classifiers. A crucial element of our approach is recognizing how to track objects throughout a video, even when they are obscured, covered or carried by other objects. Currently prevalent deep learning based methods exhibit spatiotemporal biases when applied to video-based reasoning problems. We introduce a model called Hopper that employs a unique two-staged induction mechanism for spatiotemporal event prediction, allowing it to simultaneously consider both the location and trajectory of moving objects. Our model capitalizes on an object's persistence through space and time, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through a new dataset called TVOB, which features video-based object-based reasoning with a focus on persistence. Our proposed dataset and evaluation framework evaluate an algorithm's ability to predict an object's hidden states based on its initial visible states and occlusion details. We discovered that objects that are more recently seen, moving, and experiencing partial concealment, tend to influence event predictions in a manner that is highly location and trajectory dependent. We observed that deep learning-based models exhibit notable spatiotemporal biases when applied to this data set, whereas our Hopper algorithm, which is built on a frame-by-frame transformer architecture and is guided by an object's persistence, achieves a 73.9% improvement in accuracy, surpassing previous human-based approaches, which only achieved 58.5% or 54.5% for top-down or top-down with topological reasoning respectively. Our research also demonstrates that the topological structure of an event, not the spatial arrangement of an object's visible states, plays a key role in event prediction in this data set. This paper presents a groundbreaking solution to this long-standing problem by introducing an innovative algorithm capable of consistently learning MoE model parameters for a wide range of non-linear functions. We also provide theoretical evidence to explain the algorithm's necessity, given the inherent characteristics of the MoE model. Key differences between learning from similar and dissimilar tasks are also examined, and the paper concludes by highlighting the latest developments and suggesting potential future pathways for promoting transferability in DNNs. Although business processes still play a crucial role, many modern applications rely heavily on services provided by platforms such as Google, Amazon, and Facebook.

To better understand the evolving landscape of service-oriented computing, this talk will delve into three key areas. By studying existing applications built using online services, we aim to identify emerging patterns that future innovations may rely on. This talk will use architectural examples and scenarios to illustrate the vast potential of service-based computing in managing digital assets. This knowledge can serve as a foundation for future computing systems and inspire innovative applications that leverage digital services to simplify complex tasks. This talk will cover the following key concepts:

* Introduction to service-oriented computing and its relevance to digital asset management
* Overview of popular services for managing digital assets
* Importance of collaboration platforms and infrastructure services in modern applications
* Scenarios illustrating the utilization of services for spatial awareness, data storage, collaboration, and cloud infrastructure
* Emerging trends in service-based computing and the possibility of future platform independence as online services continue to evolve. This talk will use architectural examples and scenarios to illustrate the vast potential of service-based computing in managing digital assets, aiming to simplify complex tasks and inspire innovative applications that leverage digital services.

An effective spin-orbit constant $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ is considered in the wave function, focusing primarily on quarter-filled electrons. We find that $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ correlates directly with the bare $\lambda$ and depends on electron interactions represented by the parameter $(U'-J')$, within a broad range in the paramagnetic phase, where $U'$ represents the inter-orbital interaction and $J'$ represents the pair hopping interaction. Increasing interactions within this phase causes a similar strength of $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ as the non-interacting scenario; however, beyond a certain point, interactions lead to a transition in the effective $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ behavior. At half-filling, the effective $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ is significantly reduced due to strong interactions and reorganization of electron density across the two orbitals. We explain these findings with both structural and virtual crystal field instabilities at weak and strong interactions respectively. Moreover, two potential experimental indicators of our findings are discussed: the first relates to the asymmetry of the angular dispersion relation of the Fermi arcs and the second is the degree of charge inequality $(n_1 \neq n_2)$ between the two orbitals. These indicators also show a first-order-like behavior at half-filling in relation to the pair of $(U', \lambda)$ parameters. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate the complex relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions, emphasizing the need to understand these parameters to quantitatively model and analyze 3D topological materials. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for certain size configurations using algebraic methods, and for all 2^n-1 x 2^n-1 size pairs through probabilistic methods. Finally, a comprehensive listing of all known GCM sizes is provided. The research also aims to establish the maximality of certain GCM sizes by exploring their connection to multi-dimensional Hadamard matrices. This connection is constructed via a new array, the 'exponential' array, in two-dimensional space, as well as two arrays in three-dimensional space, one of which is previously unknown. The arrays serve to establish the 'closeness' of certain GCM sizes, thereby allowing for their determination through the association of GCM with multi-dimensional Hadamard matrices. This association is achieved by discovering three-dimensional space arrays, 'wrap-around' GCM and a set of possible sizes for wrap-around GCM, thereby establishing the 'closeness' condition. This condition is also proven necessary, established as the only one in fact. As an application of the 'closeness' condition, previously unknown, low-weight linear codes and their corresponding 3-dimensional space GCM are presented. The 'closeness' condition is also exploited in a related area to discover the maximal size of, previously unknown, 3-dimensional GCM. This size is established as being unlimited. This research also aims to establish the 'closeness' condition as the sole determining factor for the uniqueness of GCM sizes in three-dimensional space.   One such innovative operating system being created as part of the HRStar project at the University of Gothenburg is ORTAL.  Built on a microkernel-based architecture with the Goal-oriented CAP approach, ORTAL is designed to integrate security, performance, and robustness seamlessly.  Our microkernel-based system incorporates several security modules such as a Security Framework, Goal-oriented Access Control, and Resource Confinement, which enforce strict real-time properties in the system.  Our microkernel architecture facilitates the decomposition of system components into primary and service modules, which shares data and functionality through well-defined, controlled interfaces.  These components are bound by strict policy constraints ensuring high-quality function integration.  Our microkernel architecture has enabled the connection of security and performance modules as shown in our previous work.  In this paper, the microkernel architecture is further developed to support the implementation of robust modules.  Our microkernel architecture is supported by a robust module interface that ensures safe and efficient interaction among modules, which is achieved through a Goal-oriented Access Control mechanism that enforces goal-related access policies, thus maintaining robustness and system reliability.  Also in this paper, we present a proof-of-concept implementation of a Resource Confinement module that uses Goal-oriented Access Control to restrict privileged operations and prevents interference and information leakage, which contributes to maintaining robustness and system reliability.  Our current system implementation has shown the effectiveness of Goal-oriented Access Control in maintaining robustness and system reliability, which can be applied to various security and non-real-time applications.  Our future work involves developing goal-oriented access control to enforce high-level security policies and non-interference properties, as well as creating a formal proof of our system's robustness and real-time properties.  The source code of our system is publicly available on the University of Gothenburg's public GitHub page.  In the future, we will adapt our proof-of-concept implementation of Resource Confinement and Goal-oriented Access Control to real-time systems and conduct a thorough evaluation of our system's performance overhead using existing benchmarks and case studies, which will be made available for public review. Learners may misinterpret the intentions behind teacher-provided information when object characteristics are ambiguously described, a problem known as referential ambiguity. We explore how principles from cognitive sciences, such as teaching strategies (tailoring instructions) and adapting to agent preferences, can mitigate referential ambiguities through induction. Our experiments involve training two artificial agents to accomplish a simulated robotic task (block-stacking) and demonstrate that incorporating these ideas increases the learner's sample efficiency. We also investigate how incorporating a preference adapter impacts the dynamics of teaching and learning within the collaborative block-stacking task. Our research reveals that teaching strategies can be tailored not only to individual learners' preferences but also to variations in sample distributions, potentially lessening the need for detailed labeling by adjusting to the learner's knowledge level. We discuss the applicability of our findings to real-world challenges in human robotics and provide an open-source codebase for reproducing our results. It enables the replication of our experiments, as well as the implementation of a novel algorithm for teaching artificial agents via natural language. Our code can be accessed via the GitHub repository at https://github.com/tss591/teaching_artificial_agents.git. We have submitted our paper for publication and the accompanying code is publicly accessible, potentially leading to further research in this area. We present our findings, such as the potential of teaching strategies and preference adapters to address referential ambiguities, as promising avenues for further investigation. We offer possible directions for further research: incorporating real-world data, developing algorithms for adaptation, and exploring the broader implications of collaborative learning. Our study, an instance of artificial cognitive engineering, has inspired a reflective examination of the principles underlying successful teaching methods. We think that incorporating ideas from cognitive sciences could render these principles more broadly applicable to human teaching as well, addressing the challenges of teaching complexity and referential ambiguity. We propose the development of a 'cognitive telescope,' a set of tools to enhance our awareness of both our own thought processes and those of others. By using the cognitive telescope, teachers can identify and rectify knowledge gaps between their intentions and students' interpretations. This paper explores the feasibility of implementing the electronic structure model using a digital quantum computer, by simulating the first excitation of hydrogen and water molecules through the sampling of one-particle density operators. We have developed an algorithm that enables the iterative construction of low-rank density matrices on quantum computers and developed implementations in Qiskit and QsysID for simulation and inverse problems, respectively. Our findings show that simulating the density matrices of hydrogen and water molecules in their ground state is achievable with a moderate number of qubits ( 4-5) but high accuracy requires quantum computation of the logarithmic part of the density matrix, which significantly constrains the available qubit sets. However, the phase estimation step poses a greater challenge, which can be mitigated through iterative low-rank updates. We also evaluated the proposed algorithm on a superconducting quantum computer for the first excited states of hydrogen and water, demonstrating that state-of-the-art qubit fault-tolerance mechanisms are inadequate for precise simulations, revealing common errors that impact results, and offering suggestions for future enhancements.
